title: Vitus
full_review:
"Vitus" (Sony Classics) is a beguiling, highly unusual fable about a 12-year-old piano prodigy (pronounced Vee-tus), first played at age 6 by Frabrizio Borsani, and then by real-life prodigy Teo Gheorghiu in an impressive film debut.

Overburdened by his musical and mathematical genius, and constricted by his loving but overprotective English-born mother, Helen (Julika Jenkins), Vitus begins to find his situation intolerable and longs to be "normal." Unpopular with the teachers and students at school because of his smart-aleck ways, he can be stubbornly disobedient at home as when, furious at the dismissal of his beloved adolescent baby sitter, Isabel (Kristina Lykowa), he refuses to budge when frustrated Helen and his father, Leo (Urs Jucker), an inventor whose company will soon do him dirt, pound on the front door.

The only place he feels truly comfortable is in the home of his eccentric but loving grandfather (Bruno Ganz), a flight enthusiast and amateur inventor himself.

Rashly attempting to fly out the window with his grandfather's wooden wings, Vitus suffers a near-fatal fall resulting in the seeming loss of his talent, and a sudden transformation to a "normal" childhood. Under the patient nurturing care of the grandfather, though, Vitus ultimately finds a way to cope with his genius. To its credit, writer-director Fredi M. Murer's script (written with Peter Luisi and Lukas B. Suter) avoids cliche.

"Vitus" was the Swiss entry for the Oscar for best foreign film and features an engaging central performance and a strong affirmation of family, not only in the boy's relationships with his parents but also with his grandfather, and a perceptive study of childhood and the albatross of talent for a gifted child.

Ganz is warmly sympathetic in a role so obviously different from his Adolf Hitler in the recent "Downfall," and there's good work from Tamara Scarpellini as the 19-year-old Isabel for whom Vitus continues to harbor a schoolboy crush, and Heidy Forster as a cheerfully unruffled piano teacher who compassionately intuits the reasons for Vitus' rudeness when they first meet.

Some deceptive actions on Vitus' part, which might be worrisome in another sort of film, are mitigated by the movie's almost fairy-tale structure, and life- and family-affirming plot resolution.

Swiss German. Subtitles.

The film contains some disrespect of authority figures including parents, deceitful behavior, insider trading, a few crude and crass words, brief underage alcohol use, and a brief reference to sex that perhaps make this most suitable for older adolescents and up. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
